title: Weigh It
context: Grade 3, the first weight topic of the metric measures chapter. An adult sees a balance being read, which a real balance and a few mangoes do well. What is actually being settled is how heavy a kilogram feels and how a thing is compared with it: a child who has only met the word kilogram believes that a bigger thing is a heavier thing, and will say that a pen is heavier than a bag of salt because the pen is longer. The tool puts the thing on the pan and lets the beam decide.

writeup.why: Weigh real things on a balance with standard weights, choose grams or kilograms for a thing, see that four equal packets make one kilogram, so two make half and one makes a quarter, and tell whether a thing weighs more or less than one kilogram.
writeup.look: A balance on a shelf with a rack of iron weights and a kitchen scale, a table of twelve real things, a Given tag that adds the weights on the right pan, an Answer tag, a unit chooser, two bins, and on the third phase four packets of sugar and a one kilogram bar.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Weigh It' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many things have been weighed or sorted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A wooden shelf runs across the top of the working area at y 214, 760 wide from x 90. On it stands a two pan balance 560 across, centred at x 380: a beam on a post, two cords and two pans, each pan 150 across, and a pointer needle at the post that swings left when the left pan is heavier, right when the right pan is heavier and stands upright when they are level. The beam tilts by the true difference in weight and never snaps. To the right of the balance, at x 700, a rack holds seven dark iron standard weights drawn as hexagonal blocks, each labelled with its weight (5 kg, 2 kg, 1 kg, 500 g, 200 g, 100 g and 50 g) and each as big as it is heavy, from 120 across down to 36, and a small digital kitchen scale 150 across whose screen shows the weight of whatever is on it. Under the left pan a deep blue Given tag 220 by 60 at x 130, y 520 adds up the weights on the right pan in kilograms and grams, and under it a green Answer tag 220 by 60 names the weight once the beam is level. The unit chooser is two round buttons, grams and kilograms, each 70 across, at x 400, y 520. The Unit fact button at x 400, y 600 (180 by 56) lays a vermilion ring round one kilogram and one thousand grams, and the Guide salt button at x 600, y 520 (160 by 56) sets the one kilogram bag of salt on one pan. The Quarter bar button at x 600, y 600 (160 by 56) shows a one kilogram bar cut into four equal quarters at x 780, y 540. A table along the foot of the area, at y 650 from x 90, holds twelve real things in their natural colours, each about 64 across with a clear gap: a watermelon, a mango, a loaf of bread, a thick book, a one kilogram bag of salt, four equal packets of sugar, a school backpack, a pencil box, a pen, a duster, a cup of yogurt and a bicycle. Two bins stand at the right of the table at x 860 and x 1010, each 130 by 130, labelled Lighter than one kilogram and Heavier than one kilogram. A note in words appears beside the Answer tag when a benchmark thing is on the pan and says about. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys for typing a weight into the answer slot. On the first phase the answer slot asks for grams or kilograms, picked from the unit chooser. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The balance shows the last thing on its pan with the iron weights that made it level, the Given tag adding them up, and the Answer tag naming the weight in green.

phases.win: the beam tilts, the chosen unit lights deep blue on the Given tag, and the Unit fact ring shows a kilogram as a thousand grams
phases.does: puts a thing on the left pan, watches the beam tilt, and picks grams or kilograms for it
phases.goal: heavy things are weighed in kilograms and light things in grams, and one kilogram is one thousand grams
phases.says: Put a thing on the pan. Is it heavy or light? Pick the unit that fits.
phases.check: Away from the screen: you hold a pen in one hand and a school bag in the other. Which one would you weigh in grams?
phases.feels: a heavy melon dipping the pan low and a pen barely moving the other one, one slow tilt at a time
phases.hands: Hold a bag of salt in one hand and a pencil box in the other, say which is heavier, and then say which unit you would use for each.
phases.tries: First rung: say whether the thing feels heavy or light. Second rung: look at the one kilogram bag of salt beside it and say which is heavier. Third rung: the same task with a thing that is much lighter or much heavier, before the full table returns.

wrong.why: a number of grams is a bigger number, so it sounds more careful
wrong.screen: the unit chooser shows the watermelon on the pan with a thousand grams drawn as ten small bags beside it, and the Unit fact ring lights round the words one kilogram

wrong.why: kilogram is the first unit met on the scale and it sounds like the right one
wrong.screen: a pen is set on the pan and the beam hardly moves, and a whole kilogram weight is set beside it to show how much heavier a kilogram is

phases.screen: a watermelon and a pen on a table, the balance level and empty, and the unit chooser showing grams and kilograms
phases.soWhat: heavy things are weighed in kilograms and light things in grams, and one kilogram is one thousand grams
phases.concept: Heavy and light: kilograms and grams

phases.win: the beam settles level and the needle stands upright, and the Answer tag names the weight in green
phases.does: drags iron weights onto the right pan until the beam settles level, and reads the weights off the Given tag
phases.goal: a balance is level when both pans hold the same weight, so the iron weights tell the weight of the thing
phases.says: Add weights to the other pan until the beam is level. What do the weights add up to?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a thing on one pan is level with a two kilogram weight and a one kilogram weight on the other. What does the thing weigh?
phases.feels: the beam leaning, then slowly coming to rest as each iron weight goes on until the needle stands up straight
phases.hands: Put a bag of rice on one side of a hanger balance and add small bags of known weight to the other side until the hanger hangs level, and say what the small bags add up to.

wrong.why: the biggest weight is the one that stands out, and it looks like the whole weight
wrong.move: reads only the biggest weight on the pan
wrong.screen: the Given tag adds the weights one at a time as the child's finger touches each one, and the total is read aloud

wrong.why: the weights on the pan look like enough, and the tilt is small

wrong.screen: the pointer needle swings a little toward the heavier pan and a thin near-black line marks where level would be

phases.screen: a parcel on the left pan, the beam tilted down on the left, the rack of seven iron weights and an empty Given tag
phases.soWhat: a balance is level when both pans hold the same weight, so the iron weights tell the weight of the thing

phases.win: two packets level against the half kilogram weight, the Quarter bar shows two of four quarters in deep blue, and the word about appears beside a loaf
phases.does: puts two packets on the left pan and a half kilogram weight on the right, then one packet against a quarter, and taps Quarter bar
phases.goal: four equal packets make one kilogram, so two make half a kilogram and one makes a quarter, and some things weigh about half or about a quarter
phases.says: Four equal packets make one kilogram. How much do some of them weigh?
phases.check: Away from the screen: four equal bags of flour weigh one kilogram. How much do two of them weigh?
phases.feels: four packets filling a kilogram, two of them balancing a half kilogram weight and one balancing a quarter
phases.hands: Share a kilogram of rice into four equal small bags with a kitchen scale, then say how much two bags weigh and how much one bag weighs.
phases.tries: First rung: how many equal packets make one kilogram? Second rung: put two on the left pan and see which weight on the right makes the beam level. Third rung: the same task with the Quarter bar showing the quarters, before the packets return.

wrong.move: says one packet weighs half a kilogram
wrong.screen: one packet goes on the left pan and a half kilogram weight on the right, and the beam dips far down on the right so the packet is seen to be lighter

phases.concept: Half a kilogram and a quarter of a kilogram

phases.win: the thing lands in its bin, the beam rests tilted the right way, and the counter reads how many things have been sorted
phases.does: puts a thing on the left pan against the guide, watches the beam, and drops the thing into the right bin
phases.goal: a thing weighs more than one kilogram when it pulls the beam down against the one kilogram weight, and less when it does not
phases.says: Is it heavier or lighter than the one kilogram bag of salt? Drop it in the right place.
phases.check: Away from the screen: say one thing in your room that weighs more than a kilogram and one that weighs less, and how you know.
phases.feels: the beam dipping down on a backpack and rising on a pen, each thing found by the way it leans
phases.hands: Hold a one kilogram bag of salt in one hand and a school bag in the other, and sort a few things from the classroom as heavier or lighter than the salt.

phases.screen: a table of twelve real things, the one kilogram bag of salt on the right pan as a guide, and two bins

phases.concept: More than or less than one kilogram

writeup.delight: On the second phase, the moment the last iron weight makes the pans equal, the beam settles with one slow bounce like a seesaw coming to rest and the needle stands straight up. On the third phase the four packets of sugar slide together into the one kilogram bar and the quarters light one by one.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet weighed. On the first phase a watermelon and a pen lie on the table, the balance is level and empty, and the unit chooser shows grams and kilograms. On the second a parcel already sits on the left pan, the beam is tilted down on that side, and the rack of seven iron weights waits beside an empty Given tag. On the third four equal packets of sugar and a one kilogram weight stand ready and the Quarter bar button is lit. On the fourth the one kilogram bag of salt already sits on the right pan as the guide, the table of twelve things waits, and the two bins are empty. One thing moves, once: the first thing to be tapped, or the heaviest iron weight on the second phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any of the twelve things on the pan, any iron weights on the other pan, the guide bag of salt, the Quarter bar and the two bins. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the unit for a pen, an apple and a sack of rice, a parcel against iron weights, loaves and bags of flour in halves and quarters of a kilogram, and a pen, a watermelon and a bicycle against one kilogram.
voiceLines: A balance, some iron weights and a table of real things. What shall we weigh first?
Put a thing on the pan. Is it heavy or light? Pick the unit that fits.
Add weights to the other pan until the beam is level. What do the weights add up to?
Four equal packets make one kilogram. How much do some of them weigh?
Is it heavier or lighter than the one kilogram bag of salt? Drop it in the right place.
A new thing for the pan. How heavy does it feel?
Free play. Put anything on the pan and add any weights you like.
Look at the beam. Is it level yet? Count the weights on the pan again.
You made the beam level, and you told heavy things from light things.

observations.why: a balance leans toward the heavier pan, and each iron weight takes away part of the difference.
observations.soWhat: a balance is level when both pans hold the same weight.
observations.observe: The beam tilted down on the side with the heavier thing, and swung back as weights were added to the other pan.

observations.why: the weight of the thing is exactly the weight of the iron weights that balance it.
observations.soWhat: the iron weights tell the weight of the thing.
observations.observe: The Given tag grew by each iron weight that went on, and the Answer tag named the same total when the beam was level.

observations.why: four equal packets fill the kilogram, so each packet is a quarter and two are a half.
observations.soWhat: half a kilogram and a quarter of a kilogram come from sharing one kilogram into equal packets.
observations.observe: Two of the four equal packets balanced a half kilogram weight, and one packet balanced a quarter.

observations.why: a thing is compared with the kilogram by its weight and not by its size.
observations.soWhat: a thing weighs more than one kilogram when it pulls the beam down against the kilogram.
observations.observe: The backpack pulled the beam down against the one kilogram bag and the pen did not.

source_tool.description: A wooden shelf at the top of the working area holds a two pan balance, 560 across, with its beam, its two hanging pans and a pointer needle at its centre that swings to the left when the left pan is heavier, to the right when the right pan is heavier, and stands upright when the pans are level. To its right a rack holds seven iron standard weights drawn as dark hexagonal blocks labelled 5 kg, 2 kg, 1 kg, 500 g, 200 g, 100 g and 50 g, each as big as it is heavy, and a small digital kitchen scale with a screen. Along the lower part of the area a table holds twelve real things in their natural colours: a watermelon, a mango, a loaf of bread, a thick book, a one kilogram bag of salt, four equal packets of sugar, a school backpack, a pencil box, a pen, a duster, a cup of yogurt and a bicycle. Dragging a thing onto the left pan makes the beam tilt, and dragging an iron weight onto the right pan adds it, so the beam tilts back by the true difference and settles level when the pans hold the same weight. A Given tag in deep blue under the right pan adds up the weights that are on it, in kilograms and grams, and an Answer tag in green names the weight once the beam is level. A unit chooser of two round buttons, grams and kilograms, sits under the left pan, and a Unit fact button lays a vermilion ring round one kilogram and one thousand grams. The one kilogram bag of salt can be set on one pan as a guide, and a Quarter bar button shows a one kilogram bar cut into four equal quarters beside the packets of sugar. Two bins stand at the right of the table, Lighter than one kilogram and Heavier than one kilogram, for sorting. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many things have been weighed or sorted.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a ruler, a measuring tape, a metre rod, a paper clip, a pencil, a book, a door, a ribbon, mangoes, a loaf of bread, potatoes, a bag of salt, a two pan balance with iron weights, a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, a glass, a teacup, a bucket, a bottle, a pot, a juice packet. The object is the thing the child measures, weighs or pours, and a plain bar or tank appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every scale is drawn with its marks evenly spaced and its zero at the edge: a ruler from 0, a metre rod in ten equal tens, a jug in equal marks, a balance with its beam level or tilted by the true difference. A reading is always taken at a mark, never between two.

Every unit is written next to its number, and a number is never written bare where a unit belongs. A unit fact is shown with both its sides, so 1 m = 100 cm is one object and one hundred centimetre marks side by side.

Converting is something the child does: a metre rod breaks into a hundred centimetre marks, a kilogram bag pours out a thousand gram dots, a litre jug empties into a thousand millilitre drops. The vermilion ring carries the times 100 or times 1000 step while it happens.
A sum or a difference is laid out in columns, units over their column, the second amount directly under the first, with a carried amount shown above the column it joins.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance. Large amounts are shown as a few tens, hundreds or thousands.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a mark or a reading the child is looking at, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a mango stays yellow and a metal weight stays dark grey. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate and is labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag and is labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from, such as one metre is one hundred centimetres, sit inside a vermilion ring and are labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag and are labelled Second or Left. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every ruler mark, scale mark, outline and plain edge is near-black, and the stage still reads with the colour taken away because each role is named in writing first.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Heavy and light: kilograms and grams
Half a kilogram and a quarter of a kilogram
More than or less than one kilogram

placement.where: After the class has held a bag of salt in one hand and a pencil box in the other and said which is heavier, and has seen a hanger balance tilt. The tool is what lets a child try any real thing on the pan and make the beam level with exact iron weights, which a hanger balance in class cannot do without a full set of weights.

answer_key.rule: Weight is how heavy something is. Grams measure light things and kilograms measure heavy things, and one kilogram is one thousand grams. A balance is level when both pans hold the same weight, so the weight of a thing is the weight of the iron weights that make the beam level. Shops keep weights of 5 kg, 2 kg, 1 kg, 500 g, 200 g, 100 g and 50 g. Four equal packets that weigh one kilogram in all mean two packets weigh half a kilogram and one packet a quarter of a kilogram. A loaf of bread weighs about half a kilogram and a cup of yogurt about a quarter of a kilogram, but only about. A thing weighs more than one kilogram when it needs more than the one kilogram weight on the other pan to level the beam, and less than one kilogram when the one kilogram weight pulls the beam down.
answer_key.wrong: The thing goes back on the left pan and the beam tilts again slowly, the weights on the right pan are counted aloud one by one as the Given tag adds them, and the beam is left tilted by the true difference. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A watermelon is a heavy thing.
Heavy things are weighed in kilograms.
Light things, like a pen, are weighed in grams.
One kilogram is one thousand grams, so a kilogram is a big unit.
items.question: A watermelon sits on the pan of a balance. Should its weight be written in grams or in kilograms?
items.checkpoint: Heavy things use kilograms and light things use grams.
items.misconception: Choosing grams because a number of grams is bigger, which sounds like a more careful answer.

steps: The pans are level, so both pans hold the same weight.
The right pan holds a 2 kg weight and a 1 kg weight.
So the sack of rice weighs 3 kg.
items.question: A sack of rice is on the left pan. A 2 kg weight and a 1 kg weight make the right pan level. What does the sack of rice weigh?
items.checkpoint: A level balance means both pans hold the same weight.
items.misconception: Giving only the biggest weight, 2 kg, and forgetting to add the 1 kg.

steps: Four equal apples make one kilogram.
Two apples are half of the four apples.
Half of one kilogram is half a kilogram.
So two apples weigh half a kilogram.
items.question: Four equal apples weigh one kilogram in all. How much do two of the apples weigh?
items.checkpoint: Half of the equal packets weigh half of the kilogram.
items.misconception: Saying two apples weigh a quarter of a kilogram, because two is a small number.

steps: Think of a one kilogram bag of salt as the guide.
A pen is far lighter than that bag of salt.
A full school backpack is heavier than that bag of salt.
So the backpack weighs more than one kilogram.
items.answer: The backpack. The pen weighs much less than one kilogram.
items.question: A full school backpack and a pen sit on a table. Which one weighs more than one kilogram?
items.checkpoint: Compare how heavy a thing is with the one kilogram bag, not how big it looks.
items.misconception: Saying the pen, because it is the longer thing on the table, when what counts is how heavy it is.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which unit fits the weight of a pen, grams or kilograms?
items.final_answer: Grams, because a pen is very light

items.question: A parcel is on the left pan. A 5 kg weight and a 1 kg weight make the right pan level. What does the parcel weigh?
items.final_answer: 6 kg, because 5 kg plus 1 kg is 6 kg

items.question: A loaf of bread weighs about half a kilogram. About how many loaves weigh one kilogram?
items.final_answer: About 2 loaves, because two halves make one kilogram

items.question: A bicycle and a pen sit on a table. Which one weighs less than one kilogram?
items.final_answer: The pen, because a bicycle weighs many kilograms

items.question: An apple and a sack of rice are weighed. Write grams or kilograms for each.
items.final_answer: The apple in grams and the sack of rice in kilograms

items.question: Put a pen, a watermelon and a bicycle in order from the lightest to the heaviest. Which of them weigh more than one kilogram?
items.final_answer: Pen, watermelon, bicycle. The watermelon and the bicycle weigh more than one kilogram

items.question: Four equal bags of flour weigh one kilogram in all. A shopkeeper puts three of the bags on a pan. How much do they weigh?
items.final_answer: Three quarters of a kilogram, because each bag weighs a quarter of a kilogram and three bags make three quarters

items.question: A parcel weighs 1 kg. On the other pan are a half kilogram weight and two two hundred gram weights. What weight must be added to make the pans level?
items.final_answer: A one hundred gram weight, because the right pan holds nine hundred grams and a kilogram is one thousand grams

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: puts a real thing on the left pan and tilts the beam by its weight
adds a standard weight to the right pan and tilts the beam back by the true difference
picks grams or kilograms for the thing on the pan
lays a vermilion ring round one kilogram and one thousand grams
sets the one kilogram bag of salt on one pan as the guide
shows a one kilogram bar cut into four equal quarters beside the four packets
types the weight of a thing, or the missing weight, into the answer slot

teaching_notes: Hold a one kilogram bag of salt in one hand and a pencil box in the other before the tool opens, and let each child say which is heavier and which is bigger, because they are not always the same thing. Hang two bags from a coat hanger as a balance and see it tilt. Say about every time a benchmark is used: a loaf of bread is about half a kilogram and a cup of yogurt about a quarter, and never ask for the exact weight of one. For the Math Lab idea, put the one kilogram weight on one pan and ask pairs to make the other pan level with different weights, then ask how many different ways were found and what each way adds up to. Wait for the child to say the beam is level before they read the weights. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's potatoes and its missing weights are the child's to work out.
generation_prompt: Build a weighing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their own natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A wooden shelf at the top of the working area holds a two pan balance about 560 across, with a beam, two hanging pans and a pointer needle at the centre that swings toward the heavier pan and stands upright when the pans are level, and the beam tilts by the true difference in weight. To its right a rack holds seven dark iron standard weights labelled 5 kg, 2 kg, 1 kg, 500 g, 200 g, 100 g and 50 g, each drawn as big as it is heavy, and a small digital kitchen scale. A table below holds twelve real things in their natural colours: a watermelon, a mango, a loaf of bread, a thick book, a one kilogram bag of salt, four equal packets of sugar, a school backpack, a pencil box, a pen, a duster, a cup of yogurt and a bicycle. Dragging a thing to the left pan and iron weights to the right pan tilts the beam, and a Given tag in deep blue adds up the weights on the right pan while an Answer tag in green names the weight once the beam is level. A unit chooser of grams and kilograms sits under the left pan, a Unit fact button lays a vermilion ring round one kilogram and one thousand grams, a Guide salt button sets the one kilogram bag on one pan, and a Quarter bar button shows a one kilogram bar cut into four equal quarters. Two bins, Lighter than one kilogram and Heavier than one kilogram, stand at the right. The running count at the top left of the canvas is how many things have been weighed or sorted. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put a thing on the left pan. Pick grams or kilograms. Add iron weights until the beam is level. Then sort the things as heavier or lighter than one kilogram.
